title: India Showcases Nuclear Advances, Development Partnerships at UN General Assembly
excerpt: Parliamentary delegation leader Sangeeta Kumari Singh Deo cited the RCA chairmanship, Kalpakkam fast breeder milestones and BIMSTEC cancer-care training, while partner nations thanked the India-UN Development Partnership Fund.
body:
• India told the UN General Assembly it backs safe, secure and peaceful uses of nuclear science, presenting itself as 'Vishwa Bandhu' — friend to the world.
  • India chairs the IAEA's 22-member Regional Cooperative Agreement (RCA) for nuclear science, a role it assumed in May 2026.
  • New Delhi cited the 500 MW Kalpakkam fast breeder reactor going critical in April 2026 and a world-first heat-based hydrogen demonstration in June 2026.
  • At the Ninth Annual India-UN Development Partnership Fund event on October 22, envoys from eight countries thanked India for development assistance.

India used the UN General Assembly's debate on the International Atomic Energy Agency report to showcase its nuclear advances and its development partnerships, reaffirming a commitment to the safe, secure and peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology. Sangeeta Kumari Singh Deo, leader of the Indian parliamentary delegation, delivered the statement at the 81st session of the General Assembly on Friday, ANI reported via NewKerala, with the Times of India also covering the address.

Singh Deo underscored the IAEA's role in helping member states build human and institutional capacity, including regulatory frameworks for peaceful nuclear applications, and India's support for the agency's Technical Cooperation Program and flagship initiatives. Framing India as 'Vishwa Bandhu', or friend to the world, she said the benefits of nuclear science should reach every nation that seeks them, backed by a robust safety and security framework.

"India's chairmanship of RCA is a reaffirmation of our strong commitment to South-South cooperation and to ensuring that the benefits of nuclear science reach every nation that seeks them."

— Sangeeta Kumari Singh Deo, Leader of the Indian Parliamentary Delegation

Chairing Asia-Pacific nuclear cooperation

India highlighted its chairmanship of the Regional Cooperative Agreement for Research, Development and Training related to Nuclear Science and Technology — a 22-member body operating under the IAEA — which it assumed in May 2026, pledging to strengthen collaborative pathways among member states through science, innovation and shared progress, according to Nation Press. As a practical example, Mumbai's Tata Memorial Centre, which operates under the Department of Atomic Energy, ran specialised cancer-care training for healthcare professionals from Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and Myanmar under the BIMSTEC cooperation framework.

Kalpakkam milestones and a generation record

The delegation pointed to two landmarks in India's nuclear programme. In April 2026, the indigenously designed 500-megawatt prototype fast breeder reactor at Kalpakkam went critical, making India only the second country to achieve stable operation of such a reactor. In June 2026, the reactor demonstrated heat-based hydrogen production, described as a world first and a potential pathway for clean hydrogen using nuclear energy. Singh Deo also noted that the Nuclear Power Corporation of India recorded generation of 55,190 million units in the previous year at an overall plant load factor of 80 percent, alongside its safety record.

Development fund draws thanks

Separately, at the Ninth Annual India-UN Development Partnership Fund Event on October 22, envoys from Laos, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, Micronesia, Moldova, Morocco and Saint Lucia thanked India for development assistance. Moldova's ambassador Gheorghe Leuca said the fund had strengthened his country's capacity to turn population data into better public policies, while Sri Lanka's Jayantha Jayasuriya said its projects respond to needs identified by the countries themselves. A Moroccan official noted the fund's record nearly a decade after its 2017 launch.

Together, the two appearances cast India's UN pitch as technology provider as much as aid partner — a positioning aimed squarely at the Global South as competition grows to shape the developing world's nuclear and development frameworks.
